title: Truth and reconciliation
hookLine: South Africa's commission heard victims and perpetrators after apartheid, imperfectly and bravely

cards: A table, a row of microphones, a room full of listeners. People who had been harmed sit down and, in public, say what was done to them and to the people they loved.
In other hearings, people who had done harm sit at a table too, and describe what they did.

This was South Africa, after apartheid ended, and the body holding the hearings was the Truth and Reconciliation Commission, chaired by Archbishop Desmond Tutu. Two words in its name, in a particular order.

teach.b: At its center was an unusual trade. The law that set up the commission allowed people who had committed politically motivated crimes to apply for amnesty.
But there was a condition: they had to tell the full truth about what they had done. Not a vague regret. The full account.
Truth was the price of amnesty. Look again at the name.

teach.h: TRUTH COMES FIRST IN THE NAME.
teach.b: Truth comes first, and reconciliation second.

For a family that had never been told what happened to someone they loved, or who gave the order, or where a body lay, hearing it said out loud could matter more than anything else the commission could offer.
Reconciliation, if it came, would have to stand on that.

Tutu kept returning to an idea in his book No Future Without Forgiveness: ubuntu, a word from southern Africa for the belief that a person is a person through other people. Who I am is bound up with who you are.
In Tutu's telling, that's why forgiveness wasn't soft or optional for a nation. If my humanity is bound to yours, your cruelty diminishes me, and your healing is part of mine.

And honesty about the result: it was imperfect, and people in South Africa and beyond still argue about what it achieved and what it left undone, about justice, about repair, about who never came forward.
The bravery and the arguing are both part of the story.
On a smaller scale it still holds: before anyone talks about moving on, the truth of what happened gets said, plainly, and heard.

how: South Africa's Truth and Reconciliation Commission held public hearings where people harmed under apartheid gave testimony, and separate amnesty hearings where applicants had to disclose fully the politically motivated crimes they had committed.

o: a person is a person through other people
a hearing where people tell what happened
a pardon given in exchange for the truth

games.q: inside the commission — tap the pairs.

s: amnesty was given to anyone who asked for it
the condition was telling the full truth about what they had done.
the commission's name puts truth before reconciliation
truth first; reconciliation, if it came, would stand on it.
everyone agrees the commission fully succeeded
people still argue about what it achieved and what it left undone.

games.q: under the old government you committed a politically motivated crime. the commission offers amnesty. what does the law ask of you?
o: the full truth about what you did.
games.why: full disclosure was the condition. truth was the price of amnesty, and the families got to hear what happened.

practice: Bring to mind one hurt, one you received or one you caused, where the plain truth of what happened has never quite been said.
Don't say it now, and don't plan a conversation; just let the truth be fully true inside you for these few minutes, without softening it.

wordCard.voice: Ubuntu. Desmond Tutu's word for the belief that a person is a person through other people, at the heart of South Africa's truth commission. Today's word.

orig.note: a word from the Nguni languages of southern Africa, written in Latin letters: humanity, a person is a person through other people.

carryVoice: Your line: truth first. Reconciliation, if it comes, stands on it. Day nine hundred seventy-two, done.
